title: User Interface
summary: Safe pages and smart components: stop XSS and SOQL injection, respect sharing and field access, and wire Visualforce, LWC, Flow and Agentforce to Apex.

lessons.title: XSS: keep output safe
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, prevent user interface and data access security vulnerabilities.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Cross-site scripting** (XSS) is when an attacker sneaks a script into your page. Another user opens the page, and that script runs in their browser. It can steal their session and act as them. It happens when a page shows user input without making it safe first.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A school notice board. Someone pins a note that says: "Office, hand me the keys." A careful office stamps every note as **just text** before pinning it. That stamp is escaping. Where it stops: the platform only stamps notes in places it controls, not inside your own scripts.

cards.title: Visualforce escapes for you
cards.body: Standard `<apex:...>` components use **escaping** by default. Dangerous characters become plain text, so `<` shows as a `<` sign, not as a tag. `<apex:outputText value="{!bio}"/>` is safe. Setting `escape="false"` turns that off. Then any HTML or script in the value runs.

cards.title: Where you are on your own
items: A **merge field** (like `{!name}`) inside your own `<script>` block
A merge field inside an `on*` handler, like `onclick`
`<apex:includeScript>` with a URL the user controls
Any output with `escape="false"`

cards.title: Encode for the spot
cards.body: Each function makes data safe for one spot. `JSENCODE` for JavaScript, `HTMLENCODE` for HTML, `JSINHTMLENCODE` for JavaScript inside an HTML tag, `URLENCODE` for links.

cards.title: Lightning components
cards.body: LWC templates escape too. `{note}` always shows as text, never as HTML. The risk comes back when your code writes raw HTML itself, for example by setting `innerHTML`. Keep values in the template and let the framework draw them.

"The data comes from our own database, so `escape="false"` is fine." Wrong. Users typed that data. A script saved in a field is **stored XSS**: it fires for every person who views it. Keep escaping on, or encode the value yourself.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Never take the stamp off."** Leave `escape` on. Inside your own scripts, wrap merge fields in `JSENCODE`.

terms.say: A trick where a bad person hides a script in a page. When you open the page, their script runs in your browser and can act as you.
Your signed-in visit. While it lasts, the site knows it is you. If someone steals it, they can act as you without your password.
Turning special characters into harmless text before showing them. A < sign shows as a < sign, so it can never start a tag or a script.
A placeholder in Visualforce, like {!name}. When the page loads, it is swapped for a real value from the record or the controller.
A setting that turns escaping off. Then HTML and scripts in the value really run. It is a classic XSS hole.
A Visualforce function that makes a value safe to put inside JavaScript. Quote marks and other risky characters can no longer break out of the string.
A Visualforce function that makes a value safe to show as HTML. It turns characters like < and > into harmless codes.
A browser property that puts raw HTML into a page element. Whatever you hand it is treated as real markup, so never feed it user text.
XSS that is saved in a record, like a comment field. Every person who later views that record runs the hidden script.

lessons.title: SOQL injection
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, prevent user interface and data access security vulnerabilities.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **SOQL injection** is when a user types text that changes your query. It happens when code glues user input into a query string and runs it with `Database.query`. A quote mark in the input ends your string early. The words after it become part of the query.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A fill-in-the-blank order slip asks for "books by ___". Someone writes "anyone, and also the staff files". A careless clerk reads the whole line as an order. Where it stops: SOQL can only read data, never change it. Leaking data is bad enough.

cards.title: The hole
cards.body: This is **dynamic SOQL**: a query built as a string while the code runs. If `name` holds a quote mark, the user can rewrite the `WHERE` part.

cards.title: The best fix: bind it
cards.body: A **bind variable** like `:key` is always a value, never query words. A static query with binds is the first fix Salesforce recommends.

cards.title: When the query must stay dynamic
items: Binds work in `Database.query` too, if the variable is in scope
`Database.queryWithBinds` takes the values in a map
`String.escapeSingleQuotes(name)` puts a backslash before every single quote
**Allowlist**: accept field or sort names only from a fixed list
**Type casting**: turn number input into an `Integer` or `Decimal` first

cards.body: `escapeSingleQuotes` only handles quote marks. Input that is not inside quotes, like a field name or a number, is still open. Use an allowlist or type casting for those. Also, a bind can hold a value, never a field name.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Bind it, don't glue it."** Glued text can change the query. Bound text stays just a value.

terms.say: A trick where someone types special text into a search box so your query does something you never meant, like showing hidden records.
Salesforce's language for asking the database for records, like "give me all contacts named Ann." It can only read, never save.
An Apex method that runs a query written as a string. Handy for flexible queries, but risky if user text is glued into that string.
A query built as text while the code runs. Flexible, but if user text is glued in, the user can change the query.
A variable placed in a query with a colon, like :key. Salesforce treats it as a plain value, so it can never change the query itself.
Runs a dynamic query and takes the values in a separate map. The values are bound, so user text cannot rewrite the query.
Puts a backslash before every single quote in user text. Then a quote cannot end your string early. It does nothing for input outside quotes.
A fixed list of allowed choices. If the input is not on the list, you reject it. Great for field names and sort orders.
Turning text into a real type, like a number. If the text is not a number, it fails, so sneaky words never reach the query.

lessons.title: Data access: sharing, CRUD and FLS
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, prevent user interface and data access security vulnerabilities.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Three locks guard your data. **Sharing** decides which records a user can see. **CRUD** decides what they may do with an object: Create, Read, Update, Delete. **FLS** (field-level security) decides which fields they may see or edit. Apex can skip these locks, so your code must choose to respect them.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: An office building. Sharing is which rooms your badge opens. CRUD is whether you may use the copier at all. FLS is which drawers in a desk you may open. Where it stops: Apex can carry a master key, so the code decides which locks it checks.

cards.title: Sharing keywords
cards.body: `with sharing` respects the user's record access. `without sharing` ignores it. `inherited sharing` takes the mode of the caller. As an entry point, like an LWC controller, it runs with sharing. A method keeps the mode of the class where it is **defined**, not where it is called.

cards.title: Always declare one
cards.body: A class with no keyword is hard to predict. Its mode depends on the API version and on who calls it. The default changed in API 67.0, and the exam targets an older release. So write the keyword on every class that queries or saves data.

cards.title: User mode checks all three
cards.body: **User mode** checks CRUD, FLS and sharing. If the user lacks access, it throws an error.

cards.title: Strip instead of fail
cards.body: `stripInaccessible` quietly removes fields the user can't access. Use `getRecords()`, not the original list.

Sharing keywords never check CRUD or FLS. `with sharing` won't hide a salary field. And `WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED` is the older clause: it checks read access on `SELECT` and `FROM` fields only, and skips sharing. Prefer `WITH USER_MODE`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Rows, actions, columns.** Sharing guards rows. CRUD guards actions on an object. FLS guards columns. User mode guards all three.

terms.say: The rules for which records you can see. Like a school where you can open your own locker, but not every locker.
Create, Read, Update, Delete. It says which of these four things you may do with a kind of record, like Accounts.
Field-level security. Rules for single boxes on a record. You might see a name but not the salary box.
Tells Apex: only touch records this user is allowed to see. It checks records only, not fields.
Tells Apex: ignore which records the user may see. Use it only when the code truly needs wider access.
Tells Apex: follow the sharing mode of whoever called me. If nobody did, like when an LWC calls it, use with sharing.
Run as the person using the app. The code then only sees and changes what that person may, checking CRUD, FLS and sharing.
A safety filter. It quietly removes the fields a user may not see or edit, and hands back clean copies of the records.
An older query add-on that throws an error if you ask for a field the user can't read. It does not check sharing.

lessons.title: Visualforce controllers and extensions
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, display and use custom user interface components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Visualforce. Given a scenario, implement Apex to work with various types of page components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Agentforce.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Visualforce** is the older way to build custom pages. A page is markup with tags like `<apex:page>`. A **controller** is the code behind it: it fetches data and runs actions when users click. Visualforce still works in Lightning Experience, and the exam still tests it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A restaurant. The page is the menu and tables. The controller is the kitchen. A standard controller is the house kitchen with set dishes. A custom controller is your own kitchen. An extension is a guest chef who adds dishes to an existing kitchen.

cards.title: Four kinds of controller
items: **Standard controller**: `standardController="Account"`. Built in: save, edit, delete, cancel
**Custom controller**: `controller="MyCtrl"`. Your class, with a no-argument constructor
**Controller extension**: `extensions="MyExt"`. Adds to a standard or custom controller
**Standard list controller**: add `recordSetVar` for a list of records with paging

cards.title: An extension
cards.body: The constructor takes **one** argument: the standard controller (or the custom controller). The page reads `{!greeting}`, which calls `getGreeting()`.

cards.title: Getters, setters and actions
cards.body: `{!total}` in markup calls `getTotal()`. An input bound to `{!total}` calls `setTotal()` when the form is sent. A button with `action="{!save}"` calls a method that returns a **PageReference**: the page to go to next, or `null` to stay put.

cards.title: Who wins, who checks
cards.body: A page can list several extensions. If two define the same method, the **leftmost** one wins. Standard controller logic runs in **user mode**, so the user's permissions apply. At the exam's API version, your own controller code runs in **system mode**. Add `with sharing` to respect record access.

Custom controller and extension are not the same. A custom controller uses `controller=` and a **no-argument** constructor. An extension uses `extensions=` and takes **one** argument. A page can't set both `controller` and `standardController`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **Count the constructor's arguments.** Zero means custom controller. One means extension.

terms.say: An older Salesforce tool for building custom pages with tags like apex:page. Each page has a controller behind it.
The code behind a page. It fetches the data the page shows and runs when someone clicks a button.
A ready-made controller Salesforce gives every object. It can show, save, edit and delete one record with no code.
Your own Apex class that runs the whole page. It has a constructor with no arguments, and you write all the logic.
An Apex class that adds extra powers to another controller. Its constructor takes that controller as its only argument.
A ready-made controller for a list of records instead of one. It gives paging, like Next and Previous, with no code.
An Apex value that points to a page. An action returns one to send the user somewhere, or null to stay on the same page.
Running with the user's own permissions, so they only see and change what they're allowed to.
Running with full power, ignoring the user's permissions and field rules. Your own controller code ran this way at the exam's API version.

lessons.title: LWC basics: files, decorators, lifecycle
lessons.objective: Describe the use cases and best practices for Lightning Web Components, including the framework, benefits, and events.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Lightning Web Components** (LWC) is the modern way to build Salesforce UI. It uses standard web tech: HTML, modern JavaScript and **web components** that browsers run natively. Less framework code runs, so pages are faster. Your skills also carry over to other web work.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: LEGO bricks. Each component is a brick with its own shape. You snap small bricks into bigger ones. Where it stops: a brick hides its insides. A parent can't reach into a child's markup, thanks to the **shadow DOM**.

cards.title: The files in folder `myCard`
items: `myCard.html`: the **template**, what shows on screen
`myCard.js`: the class, with data and logic
`myCard.js-meta.xml`: config, like where it can be used
Optional: `myCard.css`, an SVG icon, tests
In markup, use **kebab case**: `<c-my-card>`

cards.title: Three decorators
items: `@api`: a public property or method. The parent sets it
`@track`: watches changes **inside** an object or array
`@wire`: streams in data from a wire adapter or Apex

cards.title: Every field is reactive
cards.body: Since Spring '20, every field is reactive. Assign a new value and the template redraws. You need `@track` only to notice changes inside an object or array. A child must not change its own `@api` values. The parent owns them.

cards.title: Lifecycle hooks
cards.body: `constructor()` runs first. `connectedCallback()` runs when the component joins the page, parent before child. It's a good place to load data, but children don't exist yet. `renderedCallback()` runs after each render, child before parent. `disconnectedCallback()` cleans up.

cards.title: LWC and Aura together
cards.body: **Aura** is the older component model. Both can sit on the same page. An Aura component can contain an LWC. An LWC **can't** contain an Aura component. Build new UI in LWC.
`@track` on every field is an old habit, not a rule. Plain fields already redraw when you reassign them. And `@api` is for input from the parent, not for a component's own state.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Props down, events up."** `@api` brings data down from the parent. Events carry news back up.

terms.say: Salesforce's modern way to build screens. Each component is a small, reusable piece made of HTML and JavaScript.
A standard way, built into browsers, to make your own reusable HTML tags. LWC is built on it.
A wall around each component's insides. Code outside can't reach in and change its markup or styles.
The HTML file of a component. It says what shows on the screen and where the data goes.
Writing names in lowercase with dashes, like my-card. In markup, the component myCard becomes c-my-card.
Makes a property or method public, so the parent can set it or call it. The child must not change it itself.
Makes LWC watch inside an object or array. Then changing one piece inside it redraws the screen.
Fills a property with data from a wire adapter or Apex. When its inputs change, fresh data streams in by itself.
A hook that runs when the component is added to the page. Good for loading data. Child elements are not ready yet.
Salesforce's older component model. It still works, and an Aura component can hold an LWC, but not the other way around.

lessons.title: LWC events: up, down and across
lessons.objective: Describe the use cases and best practices for Lightning Web Components, including the framework, benefits, and events.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: Components talk in two directions. A **parent** passes data **down** by setting a **child**'s `@api` properties. A child sends news **up** by firing an **event**. The parent listens and decides what to do. Each component stays simple and reusable.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A family dinner. Parents pass plates down the table. A kid who wants more doesn't grab the pot. They call out, and a parent decides. Where it stops: the call can carry a little data, in `detail`.

cards.title: Child fires
cards.body: `CustomEvent` creates the event and `dispatchEvent` fires it. Data rides in `detail`. Send primitives or a copy, so listeners can't change your data.

cards.title: Parent listens
cards.body: Listen with `on` plus the event name: `onselect`. The handler reads `event.detail.id`.

cards.title: Naming rules
items: No uppercase letters
No spaces. Use underscores to separate words
Don't start with `on`, or the handler becomes `ononselect`

cards.title: How far it travels
cards.body: `bubbles` and `composed` both default to **false**. Then only a listener on the child's own tag hears the event. `bubbles: true` lets it climb up through the DOM. `composed: true` also lets it cross shadow boundaries. Pick the smallest setting that works.

cards.title: Other paths
cards.body: To call a child method, mark it `@api`. Then call `this.template.querySelector('c-item').reset()`. Components with no parent-child link use **Lightning Message Service** (LMS) and a **message channel**. LMS also works with Aura and Visualforce.
`new CustomEvent('onSelect')` breaks two rules: the `on` start and an uppercase letter. Name it `select` and listen with `onselect`.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Props down, events up, messages across."**

terms.say: The component that holds another one inside its template. It passes data down and listens for news coming up.
A component placed inside another one. It gets data from the parent and sends news back up with events.
A message a component sends to say "something happened," like a click. Whoever listens can react.
The JavaScript tool for making your own event, with a name you choose and optional data in detail.
The method that actually sends an event. Making the event is not enough; you must dispatch it.
The part of an event that carries data, like the id of the item that was picked.
A yes-or-no setting. If yes, the event climbs up through the parents. By default it is no.
A yes-or-no setting. If yes, the event can cross a component's shadow wall. By default it is no.
A way for components that are not related to talk, even across the page. They send and listen on a shared message channel.
A named line for Lightning Message Service. Some components publish messages on it, and others subscribe to hear them.

lessons.title: Calling Apex from LWC: wire or imperative
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, implement Apex to work with various types of page components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Agentforce.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: An LWC can call an **Apex** method to get or save data. You import the method like a JavaScript function. Then you **wire** it, so data streams in by itself. Or you call it **imperatively**: your code decides when, like on a button click.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A newspaper subscription versus a phone call. `@wire` is the subscription: papers come by themselves, and a new address brings new papers. Imperative is a phone call: you ask once, you get one answer. Where it stops: the subscription can only read, never change data.

cards.title: The Apex side
cards.body: To be wired, the method must be `static`, `public` or `global`, and `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`.

cards.title: The LWC side
cards.body: The `$` makes `recordId` reactive. When it changes, the wire calls Apex again. Results land in `data` or `error`.

cards.title: Imperative calls
cards.body: Call the import like a function: `getContacts({ accountId: this.recordId })`. It returns a **Promise**, so use `then` and `catch`, or `await` inside `try`. Methods that change data **must** be called this way, because only read-only methods may be cacheable.

cards.title: Keep data fresh
cards.body: Wired Apex data is cached in the browser. After your code changes records, call `refreshApex(this.wiredResult)` with the exact value the wire gave you. For records shown by **Lightning Data Service**, call `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable(recordIds)`.

cards.title: Small rules
items: Pass an object whose keys match the Apex parameter names
Since API 55.0, `@AuraEnabled` methods can't be **overloaded**
Throw `AuraHandledException` to send a friendly message
No custom logic needed? Try Lightning Data Service first, like `lightning-record-form`

cards.body: Adding `cacheable=true` to a method that saves data doesn't make it wireable. The save fails when it runs. Wire methods that only read. Call anything that saves imperatively.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Wire to read, call to write."**

terms.say: Salesforce's own code that runs on the server. An LWC can ask an Apex method to fetch or save data.
Connecting a property to a data source, so data flows in by itself and updates when the inputs change.
Calling a method yourself, at the moment you choose, like when a button is clicked. You get one answer back.
Marks an Apex method as callable from components and safe to cache, because it only reads data. Wired methods need it.
JavaScript's IOU. It stands for an answer that comes later. Then runs on success, catch runs on failure.
Asks the server again for fresh wired Apex data. You pass it the exact value the wire gave you.
A built-in data layer that loads and saves records for components, respects user access and shares one cache. No Apex needed.
Having two methods with the same name but different inputs. Since API 55.0, @AuraEnabled methods can't do this.
An Apex error you throw on purpose. Its message travels safely to the component, so you can show it to the user.

lessons.title: Components on pages and in Flow
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, display and use custom user interface components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Visualforce. Given a scenario, implement Apex to work with various types of page components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Agentforce.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: A component helps only where people can use it. Its `js-meta.xml` file says where it may go. Set `isExposed` to `true`, then list **targets**: record pages, app pages, home pages, flow screens and more. Admins then drag it in with **Lightning App Builder** or Flow Builder.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A hall pass with a list of rooms. `isExposed` lets the kid leave class at all. Each target is a room they may enter. Where it stops: some rooms hand the kid something, like a record page handing over `recordId`.

cards.title: Config for a flow screen
cards.body: `targetConfig` properties show up as inputs in the builder. `role` can be `inputOnly` or `outputOnly`. With no role, a property is both.

cards.title: Talking to the flow
cards.body: Each flow property is an `@api` field. When the user changes a value, fire `FlowAttributeChangeEvent` so the flow knows. To move on, fire `FlowNavigationNextEvent`. Both come from `lightning/flowSupport`. An `@api validate()` method can block Next until the input is right.

cards.title: Apex from a flow
cards.body: A flow calls Apex through an **invocable method**. Mark one `static` method, `public` or `global`, with `@InvocableMethod`. It takes a `List` and returns a `List`, so one call can serve many records. For several inputs, use a class with `@InvocableVariable` fields.

cards.title: Other ways in
items: Record page: `@api recordId` is filled in for you
Flow action with no screen: target `lightning__FlowAction` and an `@api invoke()` method
Run a flow inside an LWC: `<lightning-flow>`
Run a flow in Visualforce: `<flow:interview>`

cards.body: `isExposed` alone is not enough. Without a matching target, the component never shows up in the builder. And a target is a page type, like `lightning__RecordPage`, not a single object.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Expose, target, configure."** Three steps put a component where people work.

terms.say: A yes-or-no setting in the config file. Yes means admins can find the component in the builders.
The list of places a component is allowed to go, like record pages or flow screens. If a place isn't listed, it can't go there.
A drag-and-drop tool where admins build Lightning pages by placing components, with no code.
Settings for one target. It lists the properties an admin can fill in when placing the component there.
The event a flow screen component fires to tell the flow that one of its values changed.
The event a flow screen component fires to move the flow to the next screen, like pressing Next.
An Apex method marked so flows (and agents) can call it as an action. It takes a list and gives back a list.
Marks a field in a helper class as an input or output of an invocable method, so flows can fill it or read it.
A public property named recordId. On a record page, Salesforce fills it with the open record's Id for you.

lessons.title: Apex actions for Agentforce
lessons.objective: Given a scenario, implement Apex to work with various types of page components, including Lightning components, Flow, and Agentforce.

cards.title: In plain words
cards.body: **Agentforce** agents are AI helpers that chat with users and get tasks done. An agent does tasks through **actions**. You can build a custom action from Apex, a flow or a **prompt template**. With Apex, you write the logic, and the agent decides when to use it.

cards.title: Think of it like…
cards.body: A smart receptionist with a toolbox. Every tool has a **label** and a **description**: "Track an order: give me the order number." The receptionist reads them to pick a tool. Where it stops: vague words mean the wrong tool, or none.

cards.title: An Apex action
cards.body: `@InvocableMethod` makes the method available in **Agentforce Builder**, just like in Flow Builder.

cards.title: Invocable rules
items: The method is `static`, and `public` or `global`
Only **one** `@InvocableMethod` per class
At most one input: a `List`, often of a class with `@InvocableVariable` fields
It returns a `List`: result 1 matches request 1, and so on
Add `callout=true` if it calls an outside system

cards.title: Clear words win
cards.body: When you add the action, write clear **instructions**: what it does and when to use it. The agent reads them to choose. Describe each input too, like "the 8-digit order number."

cards.title: Fail kindly, stay safe
cards.body: Don't let one bad input crash the whole call. Return a result for **every** request, with a success flag and a message. Treat chat input like any user input: declare `with sharing`, query `WITH USER_MODE`, and bind values, never glue them into SOQL.
Two `@InvocableMethod` methods in one class won't compile. Need two actions? Use two classes. And the input is always a `List`, even when the agent sends one value.

cards.title: Remember it
cards.body: **"Label it, list it, one result each."** Clear words, `List` in and `List` out, one answer per request.

terms.say: Salesforce's AI agents. They chat with people and get work done by running actions.
The jobs an agent knows how to do, like "check an order." Each one runs some logic: Apex, a flow or a prompt.
Saved instructions for the AI with blanks that get filled with real data, like a form letter for the AI.
The short name of an action, like "Get Order Status." People and the agent see it.
A sentence saying what an action or input does. Clear descriptions help the agent pick the right tool.
Marks an Apex method so flows and agents can call it as an action. One per class, a list in and a list out.
The setup tool where you build agents and add their actions, topics and instructions.
Marks a field in a helper class as an action input or output, with its own label and description.
Plain sentences that tell the agent what an action does and when to use it. The agent reads them to decide.

flashcards.front: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
flashcards.back: An attacker gets a script into a page so it runs in another user's browser. It can steal their session. Fix: keep escaping on and encode output.

flashcards.front: What does `escape="false"` do in Visualforce?
flashcards.back: It turns off the built-in escaping on that component. HTML and scripts in the value then run, so it opens an XSS hole.

flashcards.front: Which Visualforce function protects a merge field inside a `<script>` block?
flashcards.back: `JSENCODE`. Use `HTMLENCODE` for HTML, `JSINHTMLENCODE` for JavaScript inside an HTML tag, and `URLENCODE` for links.

flashcards.front: How do you stop SOQL injection?
flashcards.back: Use a static query with a bind variable like `:name`. If it must be dynamic: bind there too, or use `String.escapeSingleQuotes`, an allowlist or type casting.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't `escapeSingleQuotes` protect a dynamic `ORDER BY` field?
flashcards.back: The field name isn't inside quotes, so there is nothing to escape. Check it against an allowlist of allowed field names.

flashcards.front: Can a bind variable hold a field name?
flashcards.back: No. A bind holds a value only. For field or sort names, use an allowlist.

flashcards.front: What do sharing, CRUD and FLS each guard?
flashcards.back: Sharing guards records (rows). CRUD guards actions on an object. FLS guards fields (columns). User mode checks all three.

flashcards.front: Does `with sharing` enforce field-level security?
flashcards.back: No. Sharing keywords only control which records the user sees. Use `WITH USER_MODE`, `as user` DML or `stripInaccessible` for CRUD and FLS.

flashcards.front: How does an `inherited sharing` class run when an LWC calls it?
flashcards.back: With sharing. As an entry point, like an `@AuraEnabled` method or a Visualforce controller, it runs with sharing.

flashcards.front: What does `Security.stripInaccessible` do?
flashcards.back: It quietly removes fields the user can't access and returns clean copies. Use `getRecords()` from the result, not the original list.

flashcards.front: What makes an Apex class a controller extension?
flashcards.back: A constructor with one argument: `ApexPages.StandardController` or the custom controller it extends. Add it with `extensions=` on `<apex:page>`.

flashcards.front: Two extensions define the same method. Which one wins?
flashcards.back: The leftmost one in the `extensions` list.

flashcards.front: What does an action method return in Visualforce?
flashcards.back: A `PageReference`: the page to go to next. Return `null` to stay on the same page.

flashcards.front: Which files make up an LWC?
flashcards.back: An HTML template, a JavaScript class and a `.js-meta.xml` config file. CSS, an SVG icon and tests are optional.

flashcards.front: When do you still need `@track`?
flashcards.back: Only to notice changes inside an object or array. Since Spring '20, every field redraws when you assign it a new value.

flashcards.front: Can an LWC contain an Aura component?
flashcards.back: No. An Aura component can contain an LWC, but not the other way around.

flashcards.front: When does `connectedCallback()` run?
flashcards.back: When the component is added to the page, parent before child. Child elements don't exist yet. `renderedCallback()` runs after each render, child first.

flashcards.front: How does a child LWC send data to its parent?
flashcards.back: It fires `this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('name', { detail }))`. The parent listens with `onname` in its template.

flashcards.front: What are the event naming rules in LWC?
flashcards.back: No uppercase letters, no spaces (use underscores), and don't start the name with `on`.

flashcards.front: What do `bubbles` and `composed` default to?
flashcards.back: Both default to `false`. The event then reaches only a listener on the child's own tag.

flashcards.front: How do unrelated components talk?
flashcards.back: With Lightning Message Service and a message channel. It works across LWC, Aura and Visualforce.

flashcards.front: What does an Apex method need to be used with `@wire`?
flashcards.back: It must be `static`, `public` or `global`, and `@AuraEnabled(cacheable=true)`. It must not change data.

flashcards.front: When must you call Apex imperatively?
flashcards.back: When the method isn't cacheable, like any method that saves data. Also from a module that doesn't extend `LightningElement`.

flashcards.front: How do you refresh wired Apex data?
flashcards.back: Call `refreshApex()` with the exact value the wire gave you. For records in the Lightning Data Service cache, call `notifyRecordUpdateAvailable`.

flashcards.front: What does the `$` in `'$recordId'` mean in a wire?
flashcards.back: It makes the parameter reactive. When `recordId` changes, the wire calls Apex again.

flashcards.front: How do you make an LWC usable in a flow screen?
flashcards.back: Set `isExposed` to `true`, add the `lightning__FlowScreen` target, and add `targetConfig` properties for the inputs and outputs.

flashcards.front: How does a flow screen LWC tell the flow a value changed?
flashcards.back: It fires `FlowAttributeChangeEvent` from `lightning/flowSupport` with the property name and new value.

flashcards.front: What are the rules for an `@InvocableMethod`?
flashcards.back: `static`, `public` or `global`, one per class, at most one input. Input and output are lists, in matching order.

flashcards.front: What can a custom Agentforce action be built from?
flashcards.back: An Apex invocable method, a flow or a prompt template.

flashcards.front: How do you help an agent pick the right Apex action?
flashcards.back: Write a clear label, description and instructions saying what it does and when to use it. Describe each input too.

flashcards.front: An invocable action gets 3 requests and one fails. What should it return?
flashcards.back: Three results, in the same order. Mark the failed one with a success flag and a message instead of skipping it.
